title: Measuring rate and reading rate graphs
html:
Guiding question

How can the rate of a reaction be controlled? To control a rate you need to know (1) how to measure it, (2) why particles react at all (collision theory) and (3) which conditions change the number of successful collisions per second. At HL you also describe rates mathematically with rate equations and the Arrhenius equation, and link them to reaction mechanisms.

Rates matter well beyond the lab. Industry wants the highest yield in the shortest time without sacrificing safety, because time is money. In your body, a biochemical reaction that runs too fast or too slow can be life-threatening, so a new medicine must release its active ingredient at the right rate. Cooking, cleaning, combustion in car engines and photosynthesis are all controlled by rates too.

CodeUnderstanding
R2.2.1Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
R2.2.2Particles react when they collide with enough energy and the correct orientation.
R2.2.3Rate depends on pressure, concentration, surface area, temperature and catalysts.
R2.2.4Activation energy, Ea, is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react.
R2.2.5Catalysts provide an alternative pathway with a lower Ea (Maxwell–Boltzmann).
R2.2.6–8 AHLElementary steps, rate-determining step, intermediates vs transition states, molecularity.
R2.2.9–11 AHLRate equations, orders of reaction, graphs, the rate constant k and its units.
R2.2.12–13 AHLThe Arrhenius equation, ln k vs 1/T graphs and the Arrhenius factor A.

R2.2.1 Rate of reaction and how to measure it

DefinitionThe rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Typical unit: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
rate = Δ[product]Δt = −Δ[reactant]Δt

Rate is always quoted as a positive number. A reactant's concentration falls, so its gradient is negative; drop the minus sign when you quote the rate. In practice we often follow an amount, mass or volume rather than a concentration, which gives rates in units such as g s⁻¹, cm³ s⁻¹ or mol s⁻¹.

You can follow any property that changes as the reaction goes and is proportional to the amount of a reactant or product:

MethodWhat changesExample / limitation
Gas volumeVolume of gas collected in a gas syringe or upturned buretteMg + HCl (H₂); CaCO₃ + HCl (CO₂). Gas must not dissolve much in water if collected over water.
Mass lossMass of flask falls as gas escapes (cotton wool plug lets gas out but stops spray)Good for CO₂ (M = 44); useless for H₂ (too light to register on the balance).
Colour / colorimetryAbsorbance or light transmittedReactions involving I₂, Br₂, MnO₄⁻. Not suitable when a precipitate scatters light.
Conductivity / pHNumber or type of ions in solutionNeutralizations; reactions where ions are used up or made.
Temperature changeHeat released or absorbedFe + CuSO₄ (also a colour change).
"Clock" methodsTime to reach a fixed pointNa₂S₂O₃ + HCl: time for a cross to disappear under the sulfur precipitate. rate ∝ 1/time. Gives only one data point per run.
Titration of samplesConcentration of samples removed at intervals and quenchedDiscontinuous; quenching (cooling/diluting) stops the reaction in the sample.
Exam tipIn the IB question on CaCO₃ + HCl, "gas bubbles", "disappearance of calcium carbonate" and "colour change" were not accepted as ways to monitor rate. Name a measurable quantity: mass loss, gas volume, pH, conductivity or temperature.

Which method would be least suitable for following the rate of Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)?

  1. Volume of gas in a gas syringe
  2. Loss of mass on a balance
  3. Change in pH
  4. Change in temperature

H₂ has M = 2.02 g mol⁻¹, so the mass of gas lost is tiny and barely registers on a school balance. Mass loss works well for CO₂ (M = 44.01) but not for H₂. Gas volume and pH are both good choices here.

Practical: following CaCO₃ + HCl by two methods

In class you compared two ways of following the same reaction:

CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

About 0.5 g of limestone chips is held in a small test tube standing upright in 50.0 cm³ of acid in a conical flask. Tipping the tube over starts the reaction at a known moment. In the mass-loss method the flask sits on a balance with a cotton wool bung and the mass is read every 15 s for three minutes; in the gas-volume method a 100 cm³ gas syringe is connected instead. Both are run with 1.00, 0.500 and 0.250 mol dm⁻³ HCl, then the mass-loss method is repeated with powdered limestone and with the acid warmed to about 40 °C.

PracticalPoints to explain: the cotton wool plug lets CO₂ escape but stops acid spray; temperature is recorded before and after because the reaction is exothermic; converting rates to mol s⁻¹ lets the two methods be compared.

0.500 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100.09 g mol⁻¹) reacts with 50.0 cm³ of 0.250 mol dm⁻³ HCl. Calculate the maximum mass of CO₂ that can form, in g.

n(CaCO₃) = 0.500 ÷ 100.09 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol
n(HCl) = 0.0500 × 0.250 = 1.25 × 10⁻² mol; 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol CaCO₃ needs 1.00 × 10⁻² mol HCl, so HCl is in excess and CaCO₃ is limiting (it is limiting at all three acid concentrations).
n(CO₂) = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol → mass = 5.00 × 10⁻³ × 44.01 = 0.220 g.
At room temperature this is about 5.00 × 10⁻³ × 24 dm³ ≈ 120 cm³ of gas, which is more than a 100 cm³ syringe holds; that is why the method says to stop at 100 cm³.
Why might the two methods give slightly different rates in mol s⁻¹? Predict, then reveal.
  • Some water vapour also escapes from the warm flask, so mass loss slightly over-estimates the CO₂ lost.
  • CO₂ is slightly soluble in water, so the gas syringe slightly under-estimates the CO₂ made.
  • Converting volume to moles assumes a molar volume (e.g. about 24 dm³ mol⁻¹ at room temperature), and a sticking syringe adds error.
  • The reaction is exothermic, so temperature drifts up during the run.
To convert: rate in g s⁻¹ ÷ 44.01 = mol s⁻¹; rate in cm³ s⁻¹ ÷ 24 000 cm³ mol⁻¹ ≈ mol s⁻¹.

Rates from graphs (TASSEL)

On a concentration (or volume, or mass) against time graph, the gradient is the rate. The curve is steepest at the start, when reactant concentration is highest, and flattens to zero when a reactant runs out.

  • Initial rate: gradient of the tangent at t = 0.
  • Rate at time t: draw a tangent touching the curve once at that point and find Δy/Δx.
  • Average rate: total change ÷ total time (the gradient of the straight line joining two points).
Key point · the class TASSEL checklistTangent (touches the curve once, drawn long) · Axes labelled with units · Size (use most of the grid) · Scale (sensible, even steps) · Extrapolation (to the origin where justified) · Line of best fit (smooth curve, not dot-to-dot). Make the gradient triangle large and give every rate with units.

The class tangent task (draw tangents at 0, 150, 500 and 750 s, find the rate at each, then describe the progress of the reaction) was marked on three things: tangents that touch the curve once and are long enough to give an accurate gradient; every rate with correct units; and a description that uses data from the graph at four distinct points.

Worked example · 1 · rate from a tangentA tangent drawn at t = 20 s on a graph of CO₂ volume against time passes through (0 s, 6 cm³) and (40 s, 30 cm³).
gradient = (30 − 6) ÷ (40 − 0) = 24 ÷ 40 = 0.60 cm³ s⁻¹
To describe the progress of the reaction in an exam, quote rates at several times (e.g. 0, 150, 500, 750 s) and say how and why they fall: the rate decreases because the concentration of reactant, and so the collision frequency, decreases.

A tangent to a [reactant]–time curve passes through (0 s, 0.80 mol dm⁻³) and (64 s, 0.16 mol dm⁻³). Calculate the rate at the point where it touches the curve, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

gradient = (0.16 − 0.80) ÷ (64 − 0) = −0.64 ÷ 64 = −0.010 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. A reactant's concentration falls, so the gradient is negative; the rate is quoted as positive: 0.010 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

On a volume of gas against time graph, what does the gradient of a straight line joining (0, 0) to the point where the curve first goes flat represent?

  1. The initial rate
  2. The average rate over the whole reaction
  3. The rate at the end of the reaction
  4. The rate constant

A chord between two points gives the average rate over that interval. The initial rate needs a tangent at t = 0, which is steeper than this chord.

Use the TASSEL letters to complete: a tangent should touch the curve once only, and every rate you quote needs units.

title: Collision theory and the factors that affect rate
html:
R2.2.2 Collision theory

Start with the class "do now": two equal masses of magnesium, one ribbon and one powder, are dropped into the same acid. The powder fizzes far faster. Collision theory explains why.

Particles in a gas or solution move randomly. Most collisions are unproductive. A collision leads to reaction only if both conditions are met:

  1. Sufficient energy: the collision energy is equal to or greater than the activation energy, Ea, so bonds can start to break. A head-on collision is energetic enough; a glancing blow usually is not.
  2. Correct orientation: the reacting parts of the particles must meet. For A + BC → AB + C, A must hit the B end of BC; a hit on the C end does nothing.
DefinitionThe rate of reaction depends on the frequency of successful collisions (collisions per unit time with E ≥ Ea and correct geometry). Always say "frequency" or "per second", not just "more collisions".

The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the absolute temperature (in kelvin).

For A + BC → AB + C, which collision can lead to reaction?

  1. A hits the C end of BC with energy greater than Ea
  2. A hits the B end of BC with energy less than Ea
  3. A hits the B end of BC with energy greater than Ea
  4. Any collision between A and BC

Both conditions are needed: the right orientation (A meets B, the atom it bonds to) and energy ≥ Ea. A hit on the C end has the wrong geometry however energetic it is.

R2.2.3 Factors affecting rate

Four things control the frequency of successful collisions: temperature, concentration (or pressure for gases), surface area and the presence of a catalyst.

ChangeExplanation in collision theory
Increase concentration (solutions)More particles per unit volume → greater collision frequency → more successful collisions per second. Think of marble chips in acid: more acid particles in the same volume means more hits on the chip surface each second.
Increase pressure (gases)Same number of particles in a smaller volume (higher concentration) → greater collision frequency. Has almost no effect on reactions in solution, because liquids are nearly incompressible.
Increase surface area (smaller particles, powder)More particles exposed at the surface of the solid → greater collision frequency with the other reactant. Imagine an iron nail in acid: only the surface atoms can be hit; chop it into pieces and many inner atoms become surface atoms.
Increase temperatureParticles move faster → more frequent collisions, and (the main reason) a much larger fraction of collisions have E ≥ Ea. A 10 °C rise often roughly doubles the rate.
Add a catalystProvides an alternative pathway with lower Ea → a larger fraction of collisions are successful. The catalyst is not used up.
Common mistakeChanging concentration, surface area or pressure does not change the energy of collisions or the activation energy; it changes only the collision frequency. Temperature and catalysts change the proportion of collisions that succeed.
Common mistakeAn older class matching task paired pressure with "has the same effect as increasing temperature". That is wrong: higher pressure puts the same gas particles in a smaller volume, so it acts like increasing concentration (more frequent collisions) and does not change the energy of the collisions.

Why does increasing the pressure on a reaction between HCl(aq) and NaOH(aq) not increase its rate?

  1. Pressure only affects exothermic reactions
  2. Liquids are almost incompressible, so the concentration of the solutions does not change
  3. Pressure lowers the activation energy only for gases
  4. Neutralization reactions have no activation energy

Pressure raises the rate of gas reactions by squeezing the same particles into a smaller volume (higher concentration). Solutions hardly compress, so their concentrations, and the collision frequency, stay the same.

Using collision theory, explain how an increase in temperature affects the rate of a reaction. Write your answer, then reveal the mark points.
  • Particles have more kinetic energy and move faster.
  • A greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ Ea (the essential mark).
  • Collisions are also more frequent, so the frequency of successful collisions rises and the rate increases.

Amount vs rate. When a reactant is in excess, changing its concentration changes the rate but not the amount of product (that is fixed by the limiting reactant). In the IB question where 1.0 g Na₂CO₃ was added to 0.50 or 2.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl (excess), only the total mass of CO₂ was the same. Likewise, crushing a fixed mass of CaCO₃ gives a steeper curve that levels off at the same final volume.

Other links: ethanoic acid reacts more slowly than HCl of the same concentration because it is only partially dissociated, so [H⁺] is lower (Reactivity 3.1).

Practical: the "disappearing cross" (sodium thiosulfate and acid)

Na₂S₂O₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + SO₂(g) + S(s)

Ionic equation: S₂O₃²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → H₂O(l) + SO₂(g) + S(s). The sulfur forms a pale yellow-white precipitate that gradually hides a cross drawn under the flask. The time t for the cross to disappear is the time to make a fixed amount of sulfur, so rate ∝ 1/t.

  • Concentration run: 50 cm³ of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ thiosulfate, then 40, 30, 20, 15 and 10 cm³ made up to 50 cm³ with water, each with 5 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl. Keeping the total volume at 50 cm³ keeps the depth of liquid (and so the amount of sulfur needed to hide the cross) the same.
  • Temperature run: 0.040 mol dm⁻³ thiosulfate warmed to about 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C; record the temperature after adding the acid.
  • Rinse the flask straight away (sulfur sticks to the glass and would cloud the next run) and keep the tile dry (a wet cross looks different and changes the end point).
  • Safety: avoid breathing the small amount of SO₂ given off. The residues are dilute and low-hazard.

In the concentration run, the student plots 1/t against [S₂O₃²⁻] and gets a straight line through the origin. What does this show?

  1. Rate is independent of thiosulfate concentration
  2. Rate is directly proportional to thiosulfate concentration
  3. Rate is proportional to the square of the concentration
  4. The reaction has no activation energy

1/t is proportional to the rate, so a straight line through the origin means rate ∝ [S₂O₃²⁻] (first order in thiosulfate, in HL language).

For the IA-style write-up of either practical, give the percentage uncertainty of each measurement (e.g. ±0.5 cm³ on a 50 cm³ cylinder = ±1 %, ±0.5 s reaction time on a stopwatch) and add them to find the total percentage uncertainty.

title: Activation energy, Maxwell–Boltzmann curves and catalysts
html:
R2.2.4 Activation energy and energy profiles

DefinitionActivation energy, Ea: the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a successful collision (to react).

On an energy profile, Ea is measured from the reactants up to the top of the curve (the transition state, a short-lived arrangement in which bonds are partly broken and partly formed). ΔH is the difference between reactants and products.

  • For the reverse reaction, Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH. For an exothermic reaction the reverse Ea is larger.
  • A reaction can be very exothermic yet slow if its Ea is high, e.g. N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is slow at room temperature because Ea is high, not because K is small.
  • Ea is not changed by temperature. Only a catalyst (a different pathway) changes it.

A reaction has ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ and Ea(forward) = +130 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate Ea for the reverse reaction.

Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH = 130 − (−92) = 222 kJ mol⁻¹. For an exothermic reaction the products sit lower, so the climb back to the transition state is longer.

R2.2.5 Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution and catalysts

The Maxwell–Boltzmann curve shows how kinetic energies are spread among particles at one temperature.

  • Axes: number (or fraction) of particles on y; kinetic energy on x (not "potential energy").
  • The curve starts at the origin (no particle has zero energy), rises to a peak (the most probable energy) and is asymmetric, with a long tail that approaches but never touches the x-axis.
  • The total area = total number of particles. The area to the right of Ea = particles with enough energy to react if they collide.

What does the total area under a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve represent?

  1. The activation energy
  2. The total number of particles in the sample
  3. The number of successful collisions
  4. The average kinetic energy

Every particle has some energy, so adding up all the energies' frequencies (the area) counts every particle. Only the area beyond Ea counts particles able to react.

Higher temperature (T₂ > T₁): the peak moves to the right and lower, the curve is broader, and it finishes above the T₁ curve at high energy. The total area is unchanged (same number of particles), but the area beyond Ea becomes much larger.

This is why a modest temperature rise has a large effect. In the class "do now" on H₂O₂ decomposition, raising the temperature by 20 °C (20 °C to 40 °C) more than quadrupled the rate: collision frequency rises only a few per cent, but the shaded area beyond Ea grows several-fold.

Catalyst: the curve is unchanged; a second, lower Ea(cat) is marked further left, so a larger area lies beyond it.

Exam tip · how IB marks the sketchBoth axes labelled; correct shape from the origin; curve does not touch the x-axis at high energy; Ea(cat) < Ea marked on the x-axis; for temperature, the T₂ peak is lower and to the right. To explain the effect of temperature "apart from collision frequency", mark Ea and say more particles have E ≥ Ea (greater area to the right of Ea).

For a lower temperature the reverse happens: the new curve starts at the origin with the old one, has a higher peak displaced to the left, crosses the original curve once, and runs below it towards the energy axis without touching it. Then explain: fewer molecules have E ≥ Ea, so there are fewer successful collisions per unit time. ("Molecules have less energy" or "fewer collisions" alone do not score; "chance of collision" alone does not score.)

Six changes: for each, does the curve change, does Ea move, and are there more, the same or fewer particles with E ≥ Ea? Decide, then reveal.
Change (others constant)CurveParticles with E ≥ Ea
1 Increase temperatureLower, broader, peak rightMore
2 Remove half the moleculesSame shape, half the height (area halved)Fewer
3 Add a catalystUnchanged; Ea moves leftMore
4 Reduce the volumeUnchanged (same particles, same T)Same number, but collisions more frequent
5 Reduce the temperatureTaller, narrower, peak leftFewer
6 Add an inert gas (fixed volume)Unchanged for the reacting gasSame
DefinitionA catalyst increases the rate of a reaction without being permanently changed, by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It does not change ΔH, and in an equilibrium it speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally (Reactivity 2.3).

Examples: iron in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the Contact process, MnO₂ (manganese(IV) oxide) or KI for H₂O₂ decomposition, enzymes in cells. Enzymes are proteins and lose their shape (denature) above their optimum temperature: in the class "do now", heating an enzyme-catalysed H₂O₂ mixture from 40 °C to 50 °C made the rate fall, because the denatured enzyme no longer provides the low-Ea pathway and Ea returns to the uncatalysed value.

A catalyst is added to a reaction at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?

  1. The Maxwell–Boltzmann curve shifts to the right
  2. The particles gain kinetic energy
  3. A greater proportion of particles have energy ≥ the new, lower Ea
  4. ΔH of the reaction becomes more negative

The energy distribution depends only on temperature, so the curve is unchanged. The catalyst lowers Ea, so a larger area lies beyond it. ΔH is unchanged.

Complete: a catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.

Typical exam questions and how to answer them

  • "Explain, using collision theory, why increasing temperature increases rate" (2–3 marks): particles have more kinetic energy; more collisions have E ≥ Ea (greater proportion of successful collisions); collisions are also more frequent. The energy point is the essential one.
  • "Outline how decreasing pressure affects rate" (2 marks): fewer molecules per unit volume (lower concentration); lower collision frequency, so rate falls. "More space" alone does not score.
  • "Explain the shape of a gas volume–time curve" (2 marks): steep at first because reactant concentration (collision frequency) is greatest; gradient falls as reactant is used up; flat when the limiting reactant is gone.
  • Graph sketches: a faster curve starts at the origin, is steeper and reaches the same plateau if the limiting reactant is unchanged; doubling the limiting reactant doubles the final volume.
  • Systematic vs random error: repeating with the same inaccurate gauge and averaging does not remove a systematic error.

Powdered CaCO₃ replaces the same mass of chips (acid in excess). How does the new volume–time curve compare with the original?

  1. Steeper at first and levels off at a higher volume
  2. Steeper at first and levels off at the same volume
  3. Same initial gradient, higher final volume
  4. Less steep, same final volume

Greater surface area raises the rate, so the curve is steeper. CaCO₃ is still the limiting reactant with the same mass, so the same amount of CO₂ forms and the plateau is at the same height.

title: Reaction mechanisms and the rate-determining step (HL)
html:
R2.2.6 Reaction mechanisms and the rate-determining step AHL

Most reactions do not happen in one collision. They go through a sequence of simple elementary steps, the reaction mechanism. The product of one step is often used up in a later one.

  • The elementary steps must add up to the overall equation.
  • An intermediate is formed in one step and used up in a later step, so it does not appear in the overall equation.
  • The rate-determining step (RDS) is the slowest step. It controls the overall rate (a reaction can go no faster than its slowest step, like a queue at a single checkout).
  • Kinetics can support or rule out a proposed mechanism, but can never prove it.

For the mechanism above (slow: A + C → X; fast: X + B → D + E), what is the rate equation?

  1. rate = k[A][B][C]
  2. rate = k[A][C]
  3. rate = k[X][B]
  4. rate = k[B]

Only species in the RDS (or in fast steps before it) appear. B reacts after the slow step, so it is zero order. X is an intermediate and never appears in a rate equation.

Key point · linking mechanism and rate equationSpecies in the rate equation are the reactants in the RDS, or in fast steps before it. The order with respect to a reactant equals the number of its particles involved up to and including the RDS. Species that react only after the RDS are zero order. Intermediates never appear in the rate equation; replace them with the reactants that formed them.

The overall equation tells you nothing about the mechanism. NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g) shows 1 mol of each reacting, but experiments give rate = k[NO₂]²: second order in NO₂ and zero order in CO.

Worked example · 2 · proposing a mechanismNO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g); experimentally, rate = k[NO₂]².
Second order in NO₂ → two NO₂ collide in the RDS; zero order in CO → CO reacts after the RDS.
Step 1 (slow, RDS): NO₂ + NO₂ → NO + NO₃
Step 2 (fast): NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂
Sum: 2NO₂ + NO₃ + CO → NO + NO₃ + NO₂ + CO₂ → NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ ✓
NO₃ is the intermediate. This mechanism fits both the equation and the rate law. Reasoning used in class: CO and CO₂ must be in step 2 because they are in the overall equation; one NO₂ must be re-formed in step 2 because only one is used overall; so step 1 must give NO + NO₃.
Your turn: why can't NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ be a one-step reaction? Think, then reveal.If it were a single step, that step would be the RDS and would involve CO, so the rate equation would be rate = k[NO₂][CO]. CO is not in the experimental rate equation, so it cannot be in the RDS, and a one-step mechanism is impossible.
Worked example · 3 · rate equation from a mechanism2NO + 2H₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O.
Step 1 (fast): 2NO → N₂O₂
Step 2 (slow): N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂O + H₂O
Step 3 (fast): N₂O + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O
The RDS uses N₂O₂ (made from 2NO) and one H₂, so rate = k[NO]²[H₂], third order overall. Note this is not [NO]²[H₂]² as the coefficients might suggest.

A + 3B → AB₃ has rate = k[A][B]². Proposed mechanism: step 1 A + B → AB; step 2 AB + B → AB₂; step 3 AB₂ + B → AB₃. Which step is rate-determining?

  1. Step 1
  2. Step 2
  3. Step 3
  4. Steps 1 and 3 together

The rate equation has one A and two B. Up to and including step 2, one A and two B have reacted (step 2 together with step 1 before it), so step 2 is the RDS. If step 3 were slowest, three B would appear.

2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ has rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. Step 1: NO + NO → N₂O₂; step 2: N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2NO₂. Which step is the RDS?

  1. Step 1
  2. Step 2
  3. Neither: the reaction is one step
  4. It cannot be decided

O₂ appears in the rate equation, so it must be involved in (or before) the RDS. It first appears in step 2, which together with step 1 involves 2NO + O₂: the same ratio as the rate equation.

In the presence of rhodium, 2NO + 2H₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O has rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. Step 1: NO + NO → X; step 2: X + H₂ → Y; step 3: Y + H₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O. Which step is rate-determining?

  1. Step 1
  2. Step 2
  3. Step 3
  4. All three are equally slow

Only one H₂ is in the rate equation. Steps 1 + 2 involve two NO and one H₂, matching it. If step 3 were the RDS, two H₂ would appear.

Predict the rate equation if the RDS of a reaction between A, B and C is 2A + B + C → X + Y.rate = k[A]²[B][C]. For an elementary step the orders equal the numbers of each particle in that step.
For each scheme, which species are in the rate equation? Which species are intermediates in scheme 3? Decide, then reveal (one student answered: scheme 1 = A and B, scheme 2 = A and E, scheme 3 = A and B; intermediates C, D, F; rate = k[A][B]).
  • Scheme 1: step (i) is slow, so rate = k[A][B].
  • Scheme 2: step (iii) is the first slow step and the steps after it cannot be faster than it, so treat (iii) as the RDS. Steps (i)–(iii) involve A, B and E, so rate = k[A][B][E]. The student's "A and E" missed B: the catalyst takes part in step (i), before the RDS, so it appears in the rate equation.
  • Scheme 3: step (ii) is slow; C is made from A + B in fast step (i), so rate = k[A][B].
  • Intermediates in scheme 3: C, D and F (each made then used). B is the catalyst: used in (i) and regenerated in (ii).
So the student's answer was right except for scheme 2.
Linking note · SN1 and SN2Tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1: slow ionization to a carbocation, then fast attack by the nucleophile, so rate = k[RX] (unimolecular RDS). Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2 in one step, so rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] (bimolecular). See Reactivity 3.4.

Practical link: the iodination of propanone

Propanone reacts with iodine with an acid catalyst: CH₃COCH₃ + I₂ → CH₂ICOCH₃ + H⁺ + I⁻. Experimentally, rate = k[CH₃COCH₃][H⁺]: zero order in iodine. The proposed mechanism explains this:

R2.2.7 Energy profiles for multistep reactions AHL

  • Each elementary step has its own hump (transition state) and its own Ea.
  • An intermediate sits in a trough (a local minimum) between humps: it has a real, if short, lifetime and could in principle be detected.
  • A transition state sits at a peak: it cannot be isolated.
  • The step with the highest activation energy (measured from the start of that step) is the RDS.
Common mistakeDo not confuse an intermediate with a transition state. Intermediate = trough, a species formed and used up; transition state = peak, an unstable arrangement of atoms.

R2.2.8 Molecularity AHL

The molecularity of an elementary step is the number of reactant particles taking part in it: unimolecular (one particle, e.g. A → B + C), bimolecular (two particles collide, the most common), termolecular (three particles at once, rare because a three-way collision with the right energy and orientation is very unlikely).

Molecularity applies to one elementary step and is a whole number; order applies to the overall rate equation and is found by experiment. For an elementary step (only), the orders equal the coefficients.

An intermediate sits in a trough on the energy profile; a transition state sits at a peak.

title: Rate equations, orders and the rate constant (HL)
html:
R2.2.9 Rate equations AHL

For aA + bB → products: rate = k[A]m[B]n
  • Order with respect to a reactant (m or n): the power to which its concentration is raised in the rate equation.
  • Overall order: the sum of the individual orders, m + n.
  • Rate constant, k: the proportionality constant. It is constant for a reaction at a given temperature and changes only with temperature (or a catalyst). Its value and units differ from reaction to reaction.
Key pointOrders can only be found experimentally. They are not related to the coefficients in the balanced equation (unless the reaction is a single elementary step). In the IB syllabus orders are 0, 1 or 2.

What each order means: zero order, [A]⁰ = 1, so changing [A] has no effect on rate; first order, rate changes by the same factor as [A]; second order, rate changes by the square of the factor.

Pair share: if rate = k[A]²[B], what happens to the rate when (a) [A] is doubled, (b) [B] is doubled, (c) both are doubled, (d) [A] is tripled? Discuss, then reveal.(a) ×2² = ×4. (b) ×2. (c) ×4 × 2 = ×8. (d) ×3² = ×9. The overall order is 3.

Initial-rates method. Run several experiments, changing the concentration of one reactant at a time while keeping the others constant, and compare initial rates:

Concentration × 2 gives rate ×Order
1 (no change)0
21
42

In general, (concentration factor)order = rate factor; ×3 concentration with ×9 rate is second order.

Worked example · 4 · deducing a rate equation and k
Exp[A] / mol dm⁻³[B] / mol dm⁻³Initial rate / mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
10.100.102.0 × 10⁻⁴
20.200.104.0 × 10⁻⁴
30.100.301.8 × 10⁻³
Exp 1 → 2: [A] × 2, [B] constant, rate × 2 → first order in A
Exp 1 → 3: [B] × 3, [A] constant, rate × 9 → second order in B
rate = k[A][B]², third order overall
k = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (0.10 × 0.10²) = 0.20 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
Check: experiments 2 and 3 must give the same k.
Exam tipRate data are often in standard form. Check the powers of ten carefully: a common slip is missing that one rate is ×10⁻³ while the others are ×10⁻⁴.

Using worked example 4 (rate = k[A][B]², k = 0.20 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹), calculate the initial rate when [A] = 0.050 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.40 mol dm⁻³.

rate = 0.20 × 0.050 × 0.40² = 0.20 × 0.050 × 0.16 = 1.6 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

2NO(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2NOCl(g). Doubling [NO] (Cl₂ constant) quadruples the rate; doubling [Cl₂] (NO constant) doubles it. What is the overall order?

  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 4
  4. It equals the sum of the coefficients, so 3, but only by coincidence

Second order in NO (×2 → ×4) and first order in Cl₂ (×2 → ×2): rate = k[NO]²[Cl₂], overall order 3. The agreement with the coefficients here comes from experiment, not from the equation.

Practical: orders for the iodination of propanone

CH₃COCH₃ + I₂ → CH₂ICOCH₃ + H⁺ + I⁻ (acid catalyst), with rate = k[CH₃COCH₃]x[I₂]y[H⁺]z. Volumes (cm³) are run from burettes so that the total is always 10 cm³; the clock runs until the last trace of yellow iodine disappears.

Exp2.0 mol dm⁻³ propanone0.1 mol dm⁻³ I₂1.0 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄water
12224
24222
36220
42125
520.525.5
62242
72260
  • Concentration in the mixture = stock concentration × volume added ÷ total volume, e.g. propanone in exp 1 = 2.0 × 2 ÷ 10 = 0.40 mol dm⁻³.
  • Compare exps 1–3 (propanone varied), 1, 4, 5 (iodine varied) and 1, 6, 7 (acid varied).
  • Typical result: x = 1, y = 0, z = 1, so rate = k[CH₃COCH₃][H⁺], which fits a mechanism whose RDS comes before iodine reacts (lesson on mechanisms).
  • Safety: iodopropanone is a strong lachrymator (makes eyes water), so keep tubes corked; halogenated residues go in the marked container, not down the sink.
Common mistakeTaking rate = 1/time works when the same amount of iodine is used up in every run (exps 1–3, 6, 7). In exps 4 and 5 there is less iodine to remove, so the colour vanishes sooner even though the rate is unchanged. For those runs use rate = (initial [I₂]) ÷ time; then the rate stays the same and the zero order in iodine shows up correctly.

In the iodination practical, what is the concentration of propanone in experiment 3 (6 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ in a total of 10 cm³)?

c = 2.0 × 6 ÷ 10 = 1.2 mol dm⁻³, three times the concentration in experiment 1. If the rate triples, the reaction is first order in propanone.

R2.2.10 Graphs of order AHL

OrderConcentration–time graphRate–concentration graph
ZeroStraight line sloping down; constant gradient = −kHorizontal line (rate = k)
FirstCurve with constant half-lifeStraight line through the origin (rate ∝ [A])
SecondSteeper curve at first, then a long tail; half-life increases as the reaction goes onUpward curve (parabola) through the origin (rate ∝ [A]²)

First and second order are hard to tell apart on a concentration–time graph, so in class we drew tangents at several times, plotted rate against concentration, and read the order from the shape. If rate against [A]x gives a straight line through the origin, the order is x.

Common mistakeA straight line means zero order on a concentration–time graph but first order on a rate–concentration graph. Always read the axes first.

A graph of rate against [X] is a horizontal straight line. What is the order with respect to X?

  1. Zero
  2. First
  3. Second
  4. Cannot tell without a concentration–time graph

Rate does not change when [X] changes, so rate = k[X]⁰ = k: zero order. (On a concentration–time graph, zero order would be a straight line sloping down.)

Key point · half-life of a first-order reactionThe half-life, t½, is the time for a reactant's concentration to fall to half its value. For a first-order reaction it is constant, whatever the starting concentration: t½ = ln 2 ÷ k ≈ 0.693 ÷ k. Constant successive half-lives on a concentration–time graph are a quick test for first order.

A first-order reaction has k = 2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Calculate its half-life.

t½ = ln 2 ÷ k = 0.693 ÷ 2.31 × 10⁻³ = 300 s.

Clock reactions and order. In the iodine clock practical, the time t to reach a fixed colour change is measured; initial rate ∝ 1/t, so plotting 1/t against concentration gives the order.

R2.2.11 The rate constant and its units AHL

Work out units by rearranging the rate equation, k = rate ÷ (concentration terms), and cancelling.

Overall orderRate equation (example)Units of k
0rate = kmol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
1rate = k[A]s⁻¹
2rate = k[A][B] or k[A]²mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹
3rate = k[A]²[B]mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
Worked example · 5 · unitsrate = k[A]²[B]:
k = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) ÷ (mol dm⁻³)³ = mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
Write dm³, not L, in IB answers.

What are the units of k for a reaction that is zero order in A and second order in B?

  1. s⁻¹
  2. mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
  3. mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹
  4. mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹

rate = k[B]², overall second order: k = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) ÷ (mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹. A zero-order reactant contributes nothing to the units.

Find the units of k: (1) rate = k[A]²[B]; (2) rate = k[A][B]; (3) rate = k[B]³; (4) rate = k[B]. Then reveal.(1) mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹ (third order). (2) mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹ (second order). (3) mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹ (third order). (4) s⁻¹ (first order). Shortcut: for overall order n, units = mol1−n dm3(n−1) s⁻¹.

Increasing temperature increases k (the rate equation's concentration terms are unchanged), which is why rate rises with temperature. Adding a catalyst also increases k.

The power to which a concentration is raised in the rate equation is the order with respect to that reactant; orders can only be found by experiment.

title: The Arrhenius equation (HL)
html:
R2.2.12 The Arrhenius equation AHL

Svante Arrhenius, one of the founders of physical chemistry, linked the rate constant to temperature and activation energy with an exponential equation. Think back: raising T raises the rate; lowering Ea raises the rate. The equation puts numbers on both.

k = A e−Ea/RTln k = −EaR × 1T + ln A

Both forms are in the data booklet (section 1); R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (section 2). Ea is in J mol⁻¹, T in kelvin. The term e−Ea/RT is the fraction of collisions with enough energy: it increases sharply as T rises or as Ea falls.

Taking natural logs (ln, not log₁₀) of both sides uses ln(ab) = ln a + ln b and ln(ex) = x: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, which rearranges to the straight-line form above.

Graphical method. The second form matches y = mx + c. Measure k (or a rate, or 1/time from a clock reaction) at several temperatures and plot ln k against 1/T:

  • Gradient = −Ea/R, so Ea = −gradient × R (the gradient is negative, so Ea comes out positive).
  • y-intercept = ln A, so A = eintercept. Extrapolate to 1/T = 0 (the intercept is usually far off the plotted data).
Two temperatures: lnk₂k₁ = EaR(1T₁ − 1T₂)

Rearrangements to practise: Ea = (ln A − ln k) × RT; T = Ea ÷ [R(ln A − ln k)]; A = k ÷ e−Ea/RT.

Worked example · 6 · Ea from A and k (class example)At 330 K, k = 1.30 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ and A = 4.55 × 10¹³ s⁻¹.
ln k = ln A − Ea/RT → Ea = (ln A − ln k) × RT
Ea = (31.45 − (−8.948)) × 8.31 × 330 = 1.11 × 10⁵ J mol⁻¹ = 111 kJ mol⁻¹
Worked example · 7 · the "rate doubles every 10 °C" ruleIf k doubles between 298 K and 308 K:
ln 2 = (Ea/8.31)(1/298 − 1/308)
0.693 = (Ea/8.31)(1.09 × 10⁻⁴) → Ea ≈ 5.3 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ ≈ 53 kJ mol⁻¹

Class calculation set (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Try each, then check the worked solution.

1. Calculate k at 289 K if Ea = 200 J mol⁻¹ and A = 9 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

Ea/RT = 200 ÷ (8.31 × 289) = 0.0833; k = 9 × e−0.0833 = 9 × 0.920 = 8.28 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (k has the same units as A).

2. Calculate k at 310 K if Ea = 6.30 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ and A = 1.75 × 10⁸ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

Ea/RT = 63 000 ÷ (8.31 × 310) = 24.46; e−24.46 = 2.39 × 10⁻¹¹; k = 1.75 × 10⁸ × 2.39 × 10⁻¹¹ = 4.19 × 10⁻³ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

3. Calculate Ea (in J mol⁻¹) at 298 K if k = 1.35 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ and A = 6.7 × 10³ s⁻¹.

Ea = RT ln(A/k) = 8.31 × 298 × ln(6.7 × 10³ ÷ 1.35 × 10⁻⁴) = 2476 × ln(4.96 × 10⁷) = 2476 × 17.72 = 4.39 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ (43.9 kJ mol⁻¹).

4. Calculate Ea in kJ mol⁻¹ at 311 K if k = 3.30 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ and A = 2.34 × 10⁶ s⁻¹.

Ea = RT ln(A/k) = 8.31 × 311 × ln(2.34 × 10⁶ ÷ 3.30 × 10⁻²) = 2584 × 18.08 = 46 718 J mol⁻¹ = 46.7 kJ mol⁻¹.
Note: k can never be larger than A, because e−Ea/RT is always less than 1. If you ever get a negative Ea, check whether k and A have been swapped.

5. Calculate T if k = 2.13 × 10⁻⁷ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹, A = 3.03 × 10⁷ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ and Ea = 76.3 kJ mol⁻¹.

T = Ea ÷ [R ln(A/k)] = 76 300 ÷ [8.31 × ln(1.42 × 10¹⁴)] = 76 300 ÷ (8.31 × 32.59) = 282 K. Remember to convert kJ to J first.
Extension: (1) Assuming A is constant, how much faster is a reaction with Ea = 40 kJ mol⁻¹ at 40 °C than at 20 °C? (2) At 21 °C a catalyst lowers Ea from 50 to 35 kJ mol⁻¹. How many times more molecules have enough energy? Work them out, then reveal.(1) Convert to kelvin and J. At 293 K, e−40 000/(8.31 × 293) = 7.33 × 10⁻⁸; at 313 K it is 2.10 × 10⁻⁷. Ratio = 2.86, so the rate rises about 2.9 times (with concentrations unchanged). The "doubles every 10 °C" rule (×4 over 20 °C) only holds for Ea ≈ 50 kJ mol⁻¹ near room temperature.
(2) At 294 K: e−50 000/(8.31 × 294) = 1.29 × 10⁻⁹ and e−35 000/(8.31 × 294) = 6.00 × 10⁻⁷. Ratio ≈ 464: a catalyst has a far bigger effect than a modest temperature rise.

Graph activity: OH⁻ + bromoethane

From the table (ln k = −1.709 at 1/T = 3.28 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹ and ln k = 3.122 at 1/T = 2.83 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹), calculate Ea in kJ mol⁻¹. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

gradient = (3.122 − (−1.709)) ÷ (2.83 × 10⁻³ − 3.28 × 10⁻³) = 4.831 ÷ (−4.5 × 10⁻⁴) = −1.07 × 10⁴ K
Ea = −gradient × R = 1.07 × 10⁴ × 8.31 = 8.9 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ ≈ 89 kJ mol⁻¹ (a best-fit line through all six points gives 89.4 kJ mol⁻¹).
Intercept: ln A = ln k + Ea/RT = 3.122 + 1.075 × 10⁴ × 2.83 × 10⁻³ ≈ 33.6, so A = e33.6 ≈ 4 × 10¹⁴ (same units as k). A is always a large positive number; a value such as 8 × 10⁻¹⁴ means the sign of the exponent has been lost.
Common mistakeIn class we assessed answers of "190 900 kJ mol⁻¹" and "−23 000 J mol⁻¹". The first forgot that R is in J, so the answer is in J mol⁻¹ (divide by 1000 for kJ). The second forgot the minus sign in gradient = −Ea/R (and also forgot to multiply by R). Use ln (natural log), not log₁₀, and convert °C to K.

A plot of ln k against 1/T has a gradient of −6000 K. What is Ea?

  1. −49.9 kJ mol⁻¹
  2. 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹
  3. 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹
  4. 722 J mol⁻¹

Ea = −gradient × R = 6000 × 8.31 = 49 860 J mol⁻¹ ≈ 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹. Activation energy is always positive; dividing by R instead of multiplying gives 722.

Practical: finding Ea with thiosulfate and acid

PracticalFinding Ea with sodium thiosulfate and HCl: time how long the sulfur precipitate takes to hide a spot at five temperatures (room temperature to about 50 °C, in a fume cupboard because SO₂ is released). Take k ∝ 1/time, plot ln(1/t) against 1/T, and Ea = −gradient × R.

Method details: 10 cm³ of about 0.10 mol dm⁻³ thiosulfate in boiling tube A and 10 cm³ of about 0.10 mol dm⁻³ HCl in tube B both stand in a water bath until they reach the bath temperature; B is poured into A, the timer starts, the mixture is stirred with the thermometer and its temperature read, and the clock stops when a spot marked on the beaker can no longer be seen through tube A. Do not heat above 50 °C (more SO₂ escapes); students with asthma should not do this practical, and the mixture is poured into the quench bucket, not the sink. Using 1/t in place of k only shifts the intercept, not the gradient, because 1/t is proportional to k when the same amount of sulfur is needed each time.

Using the sample results, calculate the mean time at 20.5 °C (628, 678 and 639 s).

(628 + 678 + 639) ÷ 3 = 1945 ÷ 3 = 648 s, so the rate ≈ 1/648 = 1.54 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
Evaluate: the two times at 52 °C are 94 s and 140 s. What should you do with them? Decide, then reveal.140 s is longer than the 136 s at 43 °C, which cannot be right for a hotter run, so it is an anomaly and should be excluded (or the run repeated). Using 94 s, a plot of ln(1/t) against 1/T for the four temperatures gives a gradient of about −5.8 × 10³ K, so Ea ≈ 48 kJ mol⁻¹. Including the anomaly drags it down to about 44 kJ mol⁻¹. Main uncertainties: judging the end point by eye, and the temperature drifting during the run.

R2.2.13 The Arrhenius factor, A AHL

The Arrhenius factor (pre-exponential or frequency factor), A, accounts for the frequency of collisions and the fraction with the correct orientation. It has the same units as k and is treated as constant over a small temperature range. Reactions between large, complex molecules usually have smaller A values because fewer collisions are correctly oriented.

Key pointThe Arrhenius equation splits collision theory in two: A covers frequency and orientation; e−Ea/RT covers energy.

On a plot of ln k against 1/T, the y-intercept equals ln A.
